report:
**Conclusion:** Yes—regular cranberry products *can modestly reduce* recurrent symptomatic, culture-confirmed cystitis/UTIs in women, but they are not a guaranteed preventive treatment and should not replace evaluation or treatment of an acute infection.

The strongest evidence is the 2023 Cochrane systematic review of randomized trials. It found cranberry products (juice, tablets, or capsules) reduced recurrent UTIs in women with frequent infections by about 26% relative to placebo/no cranberry. Benefits were not demonstrated consistently in all populations (for example, older institutionalized adults or people with bladder-emptying problems). Products and doses varied substantially, so there is no well-established best juice volume or extract dose.  
https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD001321.pub6/full

Guidelines therefore regard cranberry as a reasonable *non-antibiotic option*, but with limitations: evidence has historically been mixed, and formulations are not standardized. The EAU guideline discusses cranberry among preventive approaches for recurrent cystitis.  
https://uroweb.org/guidelines/urological-infections/chapter/the-guideline

**Practical implications:** A standardized cranberry extract may be more convenient than juice, which can contain considerable sugar; choose a product with disclosed cranberry/PAC content where possible. Do not use cranberry to treat fever, flank/back pain, vomiting, pregnancy-associated symptoms, or a suspected kidney infection—seek medical care. Recurrent episodes should ideally be confirmed by urine culture and discussed with a clinician, since other preventive measures (e.g., adequate fluids, vaginal estrogen after menopause, or selected antimicrobial/non-antibiotic prophylaxis) may be more appropriate.

Cranberry is generally well tolerated, but discuss supplements with a clinician/pharmacist if taking warfarin or if prone to kidney stones.  
https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/cranberry
